claims.text: Superconductivity emerges in the selected high-entropy alloy if its atomic-scale mixing is sufficiently homogeneous.
Sufficient atomic-scale homogeneity is necessary for superconductivity in the selected alloy.
The selected alloy would exhibit conventional superconducting pairing.
Atomic-scale homogeneity enables electron-phonon pairing in the selected alloy.
Elemental segregation suppresses superconductivity in the selected alloy.
Secondary phases suppress superconductivity in the selected alloy.
The as-cast alloy may contain nanoscale compositional inhomogeneities and secondary-phase inclusions.
Controlled thermal annealing can increase atomic or phase homogeneity while retaining the alloy's overall high-entropy composition.
A compositionally homogeneous lattice produces a more uniform electronic potential.
A uniform lattice potential promotes coherent electron-phonon coupling and conventional s-wave Cooper pairing.
Compositional inhomogeneities and secondary phases produce local variations in the electronic density of states.
Electronic variations associated with inhomogeneity scatter electrons and hinder formation of a superconducting condensate.
The annealed alloy will exhibit a distinct superconducting transition detectable by resistivity and magnetic-susceptibility measurements.
The as-cast alloy will exhibit either no superconducting transition or a significantly weaker superconducting signature than the annealed alloy.
High-entropy alloys contain multiple principal elements in approximately equiatomic proportions and have high configurational entropy.
The proposed mechanism applies only when annealing permits homogenization without causing phase separation or crystallographic transformation.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply below 5 K.
The proposed mechanism applies when extrinsic disorder is the primary variable controlling superconductivity.
